title: Home — Jon D. Elton
text: Jon D. Elton — Thoughts & Muses of the Man. A singer, poet, and family man. Here you will find various aspects of my life I wish to make public. The Lake House at Sudden Valley on Lake Whatcom, a favourite gathering place for all of us. D.H. Elton Poems — popular poems written by my father's father, a prolific poet who wrote hundreds of them. My Desiderata — the affirmation I recite to myself every day, things worth desiring in this life. Thoughts & Poems — a compilation of thoughts and poems I have collected during my life. title: The Elton Lake House
text: The Elton Lake House at Sudden Valley, Lake Whatcom, Bellingham, Washington. Enjoy the waterfront of beautiful Lake Whatcom — waterski, swim, kayak, canoe, or just read a book. Located at #6 Inlet Circle, Bellingham, in Sudden Valley on Lake Whatcom. A 4,200 square foot home with 5 bedrooms and 4½ bathrooms, including a self-contained suite on the lowest level. It has been a great family reunion location for our family of 6 grown children, their spouses, and 15 grandchildren. Pretty tight when we are all there at the same time — but it's great having everyone under one roof. Kind words from our friends: the Walker Family, Cordell & Marilyn Rolfson, and Merlin & Maureen Smith.

title: D.H. Elton Poems — Collection
text: Poems written by my father's father, David Horton Elton. Grandpa wrote a lot of great poems — literally hundreds of them. He wrote poems for important events in the lives of his wife and children, for his Kiwanis Club, his Liberal Party, his Church, his City. He would write a poem for a friend or neighbour in need, or an event he was asked to speak at. He was very prolific and could write a poem at least every week. Many of his poems became classics that have been memorized and passed on. The popular poems include Guy in the Glass, Life the True Poem, My Sweetheart, Teach Me to Love, My Mother, God's Choicest Gift, Three Things, and Mother Bobbed Her Hair Today. More poems are being transcribed from Grandpa's journals. Check back soon.

title: My Desiderata
text: My Desiderata — Desiderata, Latin for Desired Things. It came out of a business trip to Calgary many years ago, when I stayed with my cousin Pamela Lehto in her lovely town house. On the wall of her guest bathroom was a plaque with Desiderata by Max Ehrmann. I remembered it from back in 1971, when a spoken word version by Les Crane was played on the radio and made it to #8 on the Billboard chart of the day, #4 in Canada. I committed it to memory, and over the years found a few bits I didn't like so much that I left out, and added a number of my own thoughts — making it Our Desiderata. I recite it to myself pretty much every day, most often during my morning shower. Go calmly amid the noise and haste and remember what peace may be found in silence. As far as possible, without surrender, be on good terms with all persons. Speak your truth quietly and clearly, and listen to others, even those who can do nothing to you, or for you, for they too have their story, and you just never know. If you compare yourself to others, you may become vain or bitter, for always there will be those greater and lesser than yourself. Enjoy your achievements as well as your plans. Keep interested in your own career, however humble, it's a real possession in the changing fortunes of time. Exercise caution in your business affairs, for the world is full of trickery, but let that not blind you to the virtue there is, for many seek after high ideals and everywhere, life is full of heroism. Be yourself, especially do not feign affection or be cynical about love, for in the face of all aridity and disenchantment it is as perennial as the grass. Take kindly the counsel of the years, gracefully surrendering the things of youth. Nurture strength of spirit that it may shield you from sudden misfortune, but do not distress yourself with dark imaginings. Many fears are born from fatigue, misunderstanding and loneliness. And when facing hardships move through them quickly, for the longer we dwell on our misfortunes, the greater is their power to do us damage. Beyond a wholesome discipline, be gentle with yourself, for you are a child of the universe, no less than the trees and the stars, you have a right to be here. And whether or not it is clear to you, no doubt the universe is unfolding as it should. Therefore be at peace with God, whatever you conceive Him to be. And whatever your fears or aspirations in this busy confused world, keep peace in your soul, for all its shame, drudgery and broken dreams, it is still a beautiful world. Be cheerful, be a good friend, be forgiving, for we all need forgiveness and remember it is usually more important to the giver than to the receiver. Be grateful and show it. Be generous to a fault. Have faith, it's what gives us hope! Don't take yourself too seriously, and strive to be happy, it is a choice.

title: Thoughts & Poems
text: Thoughts & Poems is a compilation of thoughts and poems I have collected during my life. Lots of great thoughts there, and it is searchable. From favorite verses to quiet reflections, this is a growing archive of what has moved me along the way — shared here in the hope that something might move you too. A few favorites: Guy in the Glass — 'For it isn't your father, or mother, or wife, who judgment upon you must pass. But the fellow whose verdict counts most in your life, is that guy staring back from the glass.' Life, the True Poem — 'Let my life be the poem I'd write, let it plead for me day after day.' My Sweetheart — 'I see you, as in former years, 'mid laughter, sadness, joys and tears.'

title: Pottery
text: Pottery — Hands in the clay, poems in three dimensions. Why a poet makes pots: pottery found me later in life, and there is something honest about a lump of mud. It asks you to be patient, to listen, to give — and then to let go, and let the fire have the last word. Words about the wheel: clay is the most patient listener I know; a pot is a poem you can hold; centering the clay is centering yourself; if the middle holds, the rest will follow; every piece comes out of the kiln either a little more or a little less than you hoped, and both are gifts. How a piece comes to life: centering, throwing, glazing, firing. From the studio: ancient pots, neolithic pottery, a Maya polychrome vase, the everyday bowl, and the wheel that started it all.

title: Church Talks
text: Church Talks — words shared from the pulpit. As a member of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, I have been asked to give talks in sacrament meeting over the years — about ten to fifteen of them. Sacrament meeting is the weekly gathering of the congregation: a time of prayer, hymns, the sacrament, and messages prepared by members of the ward. Talks listed here include Faith, The Power of Prayer, The Atonement of Jesus Christ, Service, Gratitude in All Things, Families Are Forever, Forgiveness, Enduring to the End, The Book of Mormon, Charity, Keeping the Sabbath Day Holy, and A Personal Testimony. Details for each talk are being gathered and will appear here as they are confirmed.

title: Ambulances and Fences
text:
It was a dangerous cliff they all freely confessed
Yet the path to it's crest was so pleasant.
But over this dangerous cliff there had slipped
A duke, and full many a peasant.
Then the people all said "Something has to be done."
Thought their projects did not at all tally
Some said, "Build a fence round the edge of the cliff."
Some, "Put an ambulance down in the valley."

Well the cry for the Ambulance won the day
For it spread to a neighboring city.
A fence may be useful or not they agreed
But soon each heart was brim full of pity
For those who had slipped on that terrible cliff.
And so people on Highway and Valley
Gave pound and gave pence, not for building a fence;
But for an Ambulance down in the valley.

For the cliff is quite safe if you're careful, they said
"And when people are slipping and dropping
It isn't the fall that hurts them so much
As that terrible shock when they're stopping."
And so day after day as these mishaps occurred
Quick forth did the rescuers rally
To pick up the ones who fell over the cliff
With an Ambulance down in the valley.

Then an old sage remarked, "It's a wonder to me
Why people pay more attention
To repairing results rather than stopping the cause.
They should really aim more at prevention.
Let's stop at it's source all the mischief," said he
"Come neighbours and friends, let us rally
If we'd just build a fence, we could almost dispense
With the Ambulance down in the valley.

title: Chins Up
text:
Two men look out from prison bars
The one sees MUD, and the other STARS.
Why MUD, why Stars, when side by side?
With me I'm sure you'll soon decide.
If MUD you'd choose, or STARS you'd win,
Just mark the angle of the chin.

Chins up, for stars of hope, and trust,
Chins down for filth and greed, and lust.
Chins up for skies both bright and clear,
Chins down for sin and shame and fear.
Chins up for courage, faith and love,
Chins down for groveling in the mud.

Just what you see depends always,
Not where you stand, but how you gaze.
The "Upward look," things clearly show
The "Downward look," may never know.
So, like the man behind the bars,
Look up and see the glorious stars.

title: Have You Tried?
text:
In the struggles and strife of everyday life,
When 'tis apparently useless to try,
For you are minus all hope you'll get over the slope,
And you just want to crawl off and die;
Then's the time to say 'Scat,' and get up to the bat
And "wallop the pill" for a run.
You won't make a hit, so long as you sit
On the sidelines and squawk: "Can't be done!"

Here's a lesson for you, and Brother, it's true.
Just hear the Good Shepherd declare--
It's the best test at length, revealing the strength
Of your faith and devotion and prayer.
Poor Peter had fished, all night he had wished
Some fish to his empty nets come,
But the night passed away and the dawn of the day
Found him fishless, and dishless, and glum.

Next day, came the call, from the Good Lord of all,
And His pulpit he made in the boat,
So the fold on the shore heard the voice they adored,
As He taught them the Gospel of Hope.
When finished, said He: Peter, put out to sea,
And let down your nets at My word."
But Peter replied: "All night we have tried,
And nothing have taken, my Lord."

"But nevertheless, at Thy Holy behest,
We'll cast down our nets once again,"
And so they obeyed, and were amply repaid,
For their nets couldn't quite stand the strain.
So remember it's best when discouraged, depressed,
To go forward with colors a flying,
For the crown never sits, on the fellow that quits,
But's reserved for the ones that keep trying.

title: “If” For Girls
text:
If you can keep your beau, when girls around you
Are losing theirs, and envying lucky you,
If you can neatly dress, and yet be modest,
With just a bit of paint and powder, too.
If you can "bob" your hair, and not look foolish
If you can walk erect in modern shoes,
You'll be a right smart girl, of real good promise--
The sort of girl a chap would wish to choose.

If you can keep your lips free from tobacco--
Your finger-tips from telltale nicotine
If you can keep your nails, not over polished,
But just enough to keep them trim and clean,
If you are worldly-wise, and yet not worldly,
and keep your mental furniture in shape,
Respect your ego--without egoism,
Be what you are, and never fake, or ape.

If you can mix, and yet remain untarnished,
And not be a wet blanket, with you group.
If you can hold your own in jolly frolic,
And yet to no mean lower-level stoop,
If you can keep a sense of goodly humour,
Enjoy a joke, and join in wholesome fun,
You'll keep your beau--if ye be worth the keeping,
And joy be yours, through all the years to come.

title: “Jack-asses”
text:
Two fool "Jack-asses", one summer's day,
Tied together with a rope they say.
Were placed in a field where the hay was piled,
And left to feast, all unbeguiled.

One said to the other: You come my way,
And let me eat some new-mown hay."
But the other replied: "Get off your beat--
You come with me, so I can eat."

They couldn't agree or get together--
They simply tested, and strained their tether--
They pawed up the earth, and mulled the soil,
With no reward for their useless toil.

And, so they pulled, on either hand,
And struggled, and sweat, to beat the band.
They tugged, and lugged, and milled away,
But got no nearer the new-mown hay.

They got "Nowhere" by striving so,
But landed up in "status quo,"
When face to face, near the end of day,
They drooped their heads, and seemed to say:

We're just a couple of Jack-ass fools,
A couple of thick-skinned, stubborn mules--
Our necks are sore, we're hungry besides,
While there's plenty to eat if we'd just be wise.

Said number one: "You come with me,
Why pull apart? Why not agree?
Let's eat together as we go along,
And we'll both be filled 'ere the day is done."

So, they went together, and ate their hay,
The rope was kind, when they went one way--
They browsed contented from pile to pile,
With a cheerful bray, and a happy smile.

A lesson here, for human folks,
Who act like thick skinned stubborn mokes.
In times of doubt, distress, despair,
Let's pull together and get our share.

And Nations, too--forget your pride--
Don't strain the bonds by which we are tied:
A moral from the "Jack-ass" learn--
And pull together at every turn.

title: It Does Not Pay
text:
It does not pay
To break the Sabbath Day.
The work you feel
In Duty bound to do
Can all be done within the time
God has appointed you.

Six days for Labour--
Seventh for God, Worship, and Rest,
Do this: Obey the Fourth Command--
Trust and be blest.

title: The Oyster and the Sand
text:
Have you heard about the Oyster? It's a clammy subject true,
But there's friendly inspiration, That is good for me and you.
We could solve so many problems, And our trials understand,
If we'd only learn the lesson, Of the Oyster and the Sand.

There once was an oyster, whose story I'll tell,
Who found that some sand had got under his shell;
Just one little grain. but it gave him a pain,
For oysters have feelings, for all they're so plain.

Now, did he berate this working of fate,
That had let him to such a deplorable state?
Did he "curse out the government, call for election?"
And cry, that the sea should have given "protection?"

No! He said to himself, as he lay on his shelf,
"Since I cannot remove it, I'll try to improve it!"

Now the years rolled around, as the years always do,
And he came to his ultimate destiny -- Stew!
But the small grain of sand that had bothered him so,
Was a beautiful pearl, all richly aglow.

The tale has a moral, for isn't it grand,
What an oyster can do with a morsel of sand?
What couldn't we do, if we'd only begin,
With all of the things that get under our skin.

title: Evening Prayer
text:
Jesus, Tender Shepherd, hear me,
Bless thy little lamb tonight.
Through the darkness be Thou near me,
Keep me safe till morning light.

Through this day Thy hand has led me,
Now I thank Thee for Thy care,
Thou hast warmed me, clothed and fed me,
Listen to my evening prayer.

May my sins be all forgiven,
Bless the friends I love so well,
Take me, when I die to heaven,
Happy there, with Thee to dwell.

title: Play Up and Don't Fumble the Ball
text:
Life is a game, and life in the main,
Must be played by the rules of the game.
One may cheat for a while, and get by with a smile,
And partake of its glamour and fame.
But, I'm thinking my son, that 'ere life is done,
You will find it is best after all,
To hit the line square, be honest and fair:-
Play up, and don't fumble the ball!

There's a time to finesse, as we freely confess-
If you never lose sight of the goal.
If the master you'd be of your own destiny,
Be sure you are still in control.
If, to weakness you play, it's a dead "give away,"
You're fearful and trying to stall-
So with pluck and with grit, hit the line, never quit:
Play up and don't fumble the ball!

Whatever you do, you'll find 'ere you're through-
The right thing to do is the best.
The right can't be beat - there's no need for retreat,
If the right is your every day quest.
Let me once again say, and hope, every day,
These words you will often recall:
With vigour and vim, determined to win:
Play up and don't fumble the ball!

title: My Creed
text:
Read a little, Write a little,
Speak a little -- then
Sing a little, Serve a little,
Help your fellow-men.

Dream a little, Think a little,
Find some Work to do.
Save a little, Spend a little,
Give a little too.

Hope a little, Trust a little,
Have a heap o' Faith,
Play a little, Pray a little,
Walk a path that's straight.

Eat a little, Sleep a little,
Keep the body fit.
Laugh a little, chaff a little,
Love a little bit.

title: The Joys of Married Life
text:
The joys of married life;
The bliss of matrimony;
The comfort of a wife;
Without her - Oh! how lonely!

A baby sweet to kiss,
A mother dear to love,
Brings happiness and bliss
And peace from heav'n above.

The days may gloomy be,
Life's work with care abound,
But, once at home we're free,
With them sweet rest is found.

Cares flee as morning dew
Before the summer's sun,
Hope springs within anew,
With wife and babe at home!

title: Just Getting By
text:
I met him one morning,
As I went to town.
He was young, he was strong,
But somewhat cast down.
I greeted him thus:
"How are you, my boy?"
He answered me languidly:
"Just getting by".

Just getting by!
That's not enough.
Just getting by!
Is pretty poor stuff.
The driftwood, the derelicts,
The shiftless, the shy,
Are the fatal results of
Just getting by.

If you're "just getting by",
You're not fit for the race,
When the boys "toe the mark",
You won't find a place.
With the sprinters and winners,
You never can match.
When the gun cracks the signal --
You're left at the scratch!

The leader, the lifters,
The builders, were they
Who were doing, pursuing
Their work, night and day.
They scorned the excuses
Of wherefore and why,
And tabooed the apology;
"Just getting by".

The soul, and the source
Of Success, surely springs
From ambition, initiative,
Work -- DOING THINGS!
It is never attained by
Those who won't try,
But are simply content with
"Just getting by".

title: Son of Mine
text:
Do the Right son of Mine,
All the time.
In the light of the right
Always shine.
This test, do your best
Every day.
Never Fear, God is near,
Ever Pray.

Head Erect, self-respect,
Conscience free,
Garnish Truth and forsooth
Chastity
In your walk, in your talk,
Just be straight.
Always work, never shirk,
Keep the faith.

title: The Spider
text:
A spider was born one early spring morn,
And lived in the top of an old country barn.
He spun his web high, and looked out on the sky,
And anxiously waited for flies passing by.

But his patience gave out, for no flies came about,
So he said, "Down below I'll just go and scout,
For I hear down below that flies to and fro,
Are humming, and bumming their way as they go."

So a single line spun he went down to the Humm,
Of his victims the flies, and his work he begun.
There were plenty of flies, and bugs there besides.
So our spider concluded he'd acted quite wise.

With a new web spun, in the corner, he hung.
Grew old and waxed fat all the summer day long.

One day it is said, in circling his web,
He discovered that single thread over his head,
And remarked, "What the deuce, there's really no use.
For this bit of thread so I'll cut myself loose."

Quite forgetting that day he came down that way
From the loft where his first web was anchored to stay
So without any pause, and discarding all laws,
He severed the thread with his scissor-like claws;

"'Twas useless", he said, "By this thread to hang"
IPSO FACTO--the whole thing collapsed with a bang:
For all, right along, by this thread was made strong,
From the beam in the loft, where his first web was hung.

And the moral friend mine is the 'ere keep in line,
With the thread overhead --so exceedingly fine.
For the thread, overhead connects with God's love,
Binding mortals, secure to the great throne above.

It's Liberty, Friendship, Justice and Right,
Equality, Freedom, Mercy and Light.
It's Virtue, and Love in this mortal probation,
It's Wisdom and Truth to a World generation.

Its Confidence, Trust, in ourselves, and each other,
It's Prayer and it's Faith, binding brother to brother;
It's Service-unselfish -willing-complete,
To smooth out the path, and guide weary feet.

It brightens the Day, and points out the Way,
For those who may otherwise wander and stray.
Then, let us not sever this fine, vital thread,
But be ever sustained by the line over head.

title: Thoroughbreds
text:
Way down in ole Kentucky where the corn and 'taters grow,
In that grand old blue grass region where streams and rivers flow,
They've got some racin' hosses, jockies find 'em hard to stop,
For they want to keep on runnin' with their heads up till they drop.

They say that these are thoroughbreds, they always finish strong,
Endurance is the quality that pushes them along.
They always run for all they are worth -- free rein and lots of bit--
The way to tell a thoroughbred--you'll never see him quit.

Why can't we just be thoroughbreds and run for all we're worth,
In spite of all discouragements, and other things that hurt.
Take a lesson from the hosses--never fluke or flunk, or flop,
But lets just keep on a runnin' With our heads up 'til we drop!

title: The Woodpecker
text:
The Woodpecker knows what his beak's for and so
He cannot be fooled for a minute,
He isn't attracted by silver and gold,
To try to find out what is in it.
He stays with the job nature fitted him for,
And avoids the concrete and stone.
You won't catch him pecking at iron or steel,
He leaves them politely alone.

He does his work well, as the poor flies can tell,
He knows where they go for the winter,
With him it's a lark, to cling to the bark,
And hammer it down to a splinter.
He can hang upside down, on the square or the round,
'Twont make any difference you see,
His feet made for hanging, his beak made for banging,
At shingles or bark on the tree.

Let's all take a lesson, quit quizzin' and guessin'
'Bout things don't concern us at all-
Quit foolin' and fussin' and messin' and mussin'
But go to the bat, and play ball.
Like the woodpecker-know what to do and just so,
Make a hit and get on for a run,
Play the right alley, and score up a tally,
For there's plenty of work to be done.

If only we'd stick, through thin and through thick,
At the work we're best fitted to do,
We could all get ahead, and earn daily bread,
And journey successfully through.
But we fozzle and fret, and struggle and sweat,
And sniffle, and sizzle, and sob,
Just because we can't be like the bird in the tree-
The Woodpecker who sticks to his job.

title: Guy in the Glass
text: Guy in the Glass. We always thought grandpa had written this poem but maybe he didn't. Great poem either way. When you've got all you want in your struggle for pelf, and the world crowns you king for a day, then go to the mirror and look at yourself, and see what that guy has to say. For it isn't your father, or mother, or wife, who judgment upon you must pass. But the fellow whose verdict counts most in your life, is that guy staring back from the glass. He's the fellow to please, never mind all the rest, for he'll be with you clear to the end. And you've passed your most difficult dangerous test, when the man in the glass is your friend. You may be like Jack Horner and chisel a plum, and think you're a wonderful guy, but the man in the glass says, you're only a bum, if you can't look him straight in the eye. You may fool all the world down the pathway of years, and get pats on your back as you pass. But your final reward will be heartache and tears, if you have cheated the Guy in the Glass.

title: Life, the True Poem
text: Life, the True Poem. Let my life be the poem I'd write, let it plead for me day after day. Never mind what my pen may indite, never mind what my feeble lips say. What I do is a heart-felt refrain. What I am is the standard and test. The rhythm of action is plain, the poem I live is the best. Let me BE let me DO let me LIVE, the poem my LIFE may inspire. Let me Strive, let me Serve, let me GIVE, the Highest my Soul can Desire. By David H. Elton.

title: My Sweetheart
text: My Sweetheart. I see you, as in former years, 'mid laughter, sadness, joys and tears, through shade and sunshine, faith and fears, the star of hope — time but endears — MY SWEETHEART. And babies, as the years roll on, with merry chatter, cheery song, have helped us on the way along, recalling days when we were young — MY SWEETHEART. I sometimes wonder how we'd fare, if we were just a childless pair, no boys or girls our lives to share, no children, dear, to love and care — MY SWEETHEART. It seems to me we'd miss a heap of real joy, and gladness sweet, which only boys and girls entreat, to help o'ercome the cares we meet — MY SWEETHEART. You're still as sweet, so runs my plea, as that blest day in Tennessee, when just Seventeen you did agree, to have this photo made for me — MY SWEETHEART. I've cherished it through all the years, faith's precious gift, dispelling fears, symbol of love — life's glad arrears, hope's blessed rainbow through the tears — MY SWEETHEART.

title: Teach Me to Love
text: Teach Me to Love. Four little words, a simple phrase, that falls like dew on sleeping flower, or like the sun's effulgent rays, bestowing service every hour. For in these simple words, I find the light and wisdom from above — the essence of all good, combined in these four words: Teach me to love. Teach me to love with heart sincere, devoid of all dissimulation. A love that gladly volunteers to serve, without remuneration. For in such love, as I conclude, we lift our thoughts to heaven above in gentle, joyful rectitude expressed in faith: Teach me to love. Teach me to love, both here and now, humanity as one great whole. Who waits upon the when and how will lose the race and miss the goal. Loving and serving, day by day, with humble grace, in semblance of our hope — the light, the truth, the way, still guided by: Teach me to love.

title: My Mother
text: My Mother. Guardian of Baby-hood, Boy-hood, and Youth. Champion of Virtue, and Honour and Truth. Friend of my Manhood — eternal friend, aye, her spirit and influence bless me, each day — MY MOTHER. In the Mansions of Glory, a friend is she. With the Sanctified Hosts she is pleading for me. She links me with Heaven, with God, and His will, she was always my friend and my friend she is still — MY MOTHER. Death does not finish her mission of Love, she zealously labours in regions above — there through all time and eternity, her love shall endure, and forever she'll be — MY MOTHER. By D.H. Elton, 1935. This is a photo of Isabella Amelia Elton with her son Hyrum, Grandpa's brother, and his two daughters.

title: God's Choicest Gift
text: God's Choicest Gift. God gave us the Sunshine, the Rain, and the Showers, He gave us the Springtime, the Fields, and the Flowers. He gave us the Summer, the birds on the wing. He gave them their Music, He taught them to Sing. He gave us the Seasons, in order they roll — the Autumn, the Winter, perfecting the whole. All Nature declaring His Glory and Power, with the sweet singing bird, and the blossoming flower. But the Choicest of Gifts, by His bounteous hand given, the finest bestowed in Earth or in Heaven, is the great Mother-love, I'm sure there's no other, as needful, and helpful, and faithful, as MOTHER. 1930.

title: Three Things
text: Three Things. Written for my youngest son, John Dalton Elton, on the occasion of his 14th Birthday, February 27th, 1934, at home. Born February 27th, 1920. Three things, my son, to help you on. They all come from within. The first I'll state, a virtue great, is called SELF-DISCIPLINE. For number two, I transmit you, a grace none should neglect — just like its mate, a grand estate, we'll call it SELF-RESPECT. And number three, you'll plainly see, cast in the self same mold — a moral will to conquer ill, is rightly SELF-CONTROL. Keep these in mind, and you will find true happiness and joy. They'll premiums pay in every way, big dividends, my boy.

title: Mother Bobbed Her Hair Today
text: Mother Bobbed Her Hair Today. These verses were written to my daughter, Viva, then in Bangor, Maine, U.S.A., February 12th, 1925 — the day of the decapitation. Mother bobbed her hair today, yes, she did, and daughter, say don't let on, but really she doesn't look too bad to me. Sort of curious like, by heck, where the clippers trimmed her neck, don't know yet just what to say: mother bobbed her hair today. She came in the parlour, stood beside my easy chair, sort o' stroked me on the chin, then she gently started in: Dearie, do you like my hair? I looked 'round with solemn stare; couldn't tell if I'd been shot, whether it was bobbed or not. Then she laughed, I looked again; sure enough, it was quite plain. Tresses gone, I changed my mind — dinky, kinky curls behind. Made out I was sore and vexed, angry, hurt, and much perplexed. But 'twas done, what could I say: mother bobbed her hair today. Why do women bob their hair? Don't ask me, for I declare I don't know, but here's some guesses why they bob their pretty tresses; maybe it's because they're fearful they'll be called old Rip Van Winkle, covered wagon, horse and mane, or some prehistoric Jane. Then they come to you, confessing that it saves a lot of dressing; night and morning, so 'tis said, all they do is shake their head.
